title: Phasors and Impedance
notes:
Activity "Phasors and Impedance" (PHY/EGR 3120), on the phasors Tool. Part 1 adds two same-frequency sinusoids as phasors (Sum Mode): the resultant of two phasors 90° apart by Pythagoras, a check against the drawn resultant, the resultant of two 120° apart by the law of cosines, a choice on the in-phase and out-of-phase extremes, and a free-text why. Part 2 (Circuit Mode, series RC) and Part 3 (series RLC) each work the chain Z → I → V_k by hand, revealing Z_total, then I, then the device voltages with the KVL closure. Part 2 closes on the Fourier link (V_C/V_in = 1/(1 + jωRC), its cutoff f_c = ω_c/2π, and a sweep of ω across ω_c); Part 3 on resonance (sweep to ∠Z = 0, compare ω₀ with 1/√(LC)) and a free-text why.

Task prompts and Hints are HTML prose, with subscripts as <sub> (V<sub>R</sub>, Z<sub>total</sub>) or Unicode digits (V₀, φ₂), and may use \( \) math. Question prompts and choices name each quantity as the Tool's Controls and readouts do (V_R, f_c, ω₀), since a Question prompt is its field's name.

Conditions, numeric and choice keys are encoded answer keys (framework/v1/authoring/encode-keys.html, or encodeKey() from framework/v1/runner/keys.js); decode one with decodeKey(). The keys agree with the engine (tests/unit/phasors/activity.test.js checks them against sum()). Tolerances: amplitudes 2% relative; phases ±2° judged mod 360°, so −270° and 90° both pass. Hints guide and never state the passing value. Points: 1 per Task with a Condition, none for a Task without one, 1 per graded Question.

parts.title: Part 1: Sum
parts.notes: The Setup fixes ω and v₁ = 3∠0°, v₂ = 4∠90° V; the first Task locks every way of changing them (the number inputs and drag handles for A₁, φ₁, A₂ and φ₂: A1, phi1, A2, phi2, tip1, tip2, crest1, crest2; and omega). The 120° Task opens φ₂ alone and its Condition checks φ₂ = 120°, so every student works the same second sum. Each compute Task hides the resultant layer (the Sum Mode's layers in ../layers.js), and the Task after it shows it; the extremes Task opens the sinusoids for dragging.

tasks.title: Two phasors 90° apart
tasks.prompt: The Tool shows v₁ = 3 cos(ωt) V and v₂ = 4 cos(ωt + 90°) V at ω = 1000 rad/s. Their phasors are v₁ = 3∠0° V and v₂ = 4∠90° V, drawn head-to-tail on the complex plane. The sum v₁ + v₂ is another sinusoid A cos(ωt + φ), and its phasor A∠φ is the vector sum of the two. The resultant is hidden: compute A and φ by hand, then submit to see it.

hint.text: The two phasors are the legs of a right triangle, and the resultant is its hypotenuse. v₁ lies along the real axis, so φ is the angle at the origin: tan φ = (the leg opposite it) / (the leg next to it).

tasks.title: Check against the resultant
tasks.prompt: The resultant v₁ + v₂ is now drawn on both Displays: check your A and φ against its readout. Then press Play, or drag the time cursor, and watch each phasor's projection on the real axis.

questions.prompt: How does the sum curve relate to v₁(t) and v₂(t)?

choices.text: At every instant it is v₁(t) + v₂(t): the resultant's projection is the sum of the two projections.
At every instant it follows the larger of v₁(t) and v₂(t).
Its peaks reach A₁ + A₂, since the two crests add.
It oscillates at twice ω, since two sinusoids are added.

tasks.title: Two phasors 120° apart
tasks.prompt: The φ₂ box is now unlocked: set φ₂ to 120°, so v₂ = 4∠120° V. The resultant is hidden again. Compute A by the law of cosines, \(A^2 = A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos(\varphi_2 - \varphi_1)\), and φ from the components: add the real parts and the imaginary parts of v₁ and v₂. Submit with φ₂ at 120°.

hint.text: cos 120° is negative, so the second phasor shortens the sum. For φ: v₂ = 4 cos 120° + j·4 sin 120°; add v₁'s real part to its real part, then take the angle of the sum. Its real part is positive, so φ is between 0° and 90°.

tasks.title: In phase and out of phase
tasks.prompt: The resultant is shown again, and the sinusoids are unlocked: drag the phasor tips or the crests, or type in the boxes. Try φ₂ = φ₁ (in phase) and φ₂ = φ₁ + 180° (out of phase).

questions.prompt: What is the amplitude A of v₁ + v₂ at the two extremes?

choices.text: In phase, A = A₁ + A₂; out of phase, A = |A₁ − A₂|.
In phase, A = |A₁ − A₂|; out of phase, A = A₁ + A₂.
In phase, A = A₁ + A₂; out of phase, A = 0.
A = √(A₁² + A₂²) at both, whatever the phases.

questions.prompt: Why is the sum of two sinusoids of the same frequency another sinusoid at that same frequency? Use the phasor picture.

parts.title: Part 2: Series RC
parts.notes: The Setup fixes every circuit value; the first Task locks the Setup Controls (includeR, includeL, includeC, V0, R, L, C, omega) and hides every revealable circuit layer (the Circuit Mode's layers in ../layers.js); the next Tasks show Z_total, then I, then V_R, V_L, V_C and the KVL closure, each right after the Task that computes it. |I| is entered in mA. The Setup gives a right triangle: Z = 300 − j400 Ω (3-4-5) at ω/ω_c = 0.75. The sweep Task opens ω alone; its Condition needs ω below 400 and above 4000 rad/s (a factor of 3 beyond ω_c = 1333 rad/s each way, from the omegaMin/omegaMax State).

tasks.title: The impedance Z
tasks.prompt: The loop is V₀ = 10 V at ω = 1000 rad/s driving R = 300 Ω in series with C = 2.5 µF (L is off). Each element has an impedance: Z<sub>R</sub> = R, Z<sub>L</sub> = jωL and Z<sub>C</sub> = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC). In series they add, Z = Z<sub>R</sub> + Z<sub>C</sub>. Z<sub>total</sub>, the current and the device voltages are hidden: compute Z in rectangular form (real and imaginary parts) and in polar form (magnitude and angle), then submit to see Z<sub>total</sub>.

hint.text: The capacitor's reactance is 1/(ωC), with ω in rad/s and C in farads (1 µF = 10⁻⁶ F). Z<sub>C</sub> points down the imaginary axis, so Im Z is negative and ∠Z is below 0°.

tasks.title: The current I
tasks.prompt: Z<sub>total</sub> is now drawn on the impedance plane: check your Z against its readout. The source is the phase reference, V<sub>in</sub> = 10∠0° V. Compute the current I = V<sub>in</sub> / Z: divide the magnitudes and subtract the angles. Submit to see I.

hint.text: Dividing by Z subtracts ∠Z, so a negative ∠Z gives the current a positive angle: it leads the source. Give |I| in milliamps (1 A = 1000 mA).

tasks.title: The device voltages
tasks.prompt: I is now drawn on the phasor plane. Each device's voltage is V<sub>k</sub> = I·Z<sub>k</sub>: multiply the magnitudes and add the angles. Compute V<sub>R</sub> and V<sub>C</sub>, then submit to see them, head to tail with the KVL closure V<sub>R</sub> + V<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>in</sub>.

hint.text: Z<sub>R</sub> = 300∠0° Ω and Z<sub>C</sub> = 400∠−90° Ω. Use I in amps when you multiply, so the voltages come out in volts.

tasks.title: Phase against the current
tasks.prompt: V<sub>R</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> are now drawn, closing on V<sub>in</sub>. Compare each one's angle with ∠I, and press Play to watch v<sub>R</sub>(t) and v<sub>C</sub>(t) against i(t).

questions.prompt: How do V_R and V_C sit against the current I?

choices.text: V_R is in phase with I, and V_C lags I by 90°.
V_R is in phase with I, and V_C leads I by 90°.
V_R is in phase with V_in, and V_C is 180° from V_in.
Both lag I by ∠Z.

tasks.title: The low-pass filter
tasks.prompt: Taking the output across the capacitor makes this loop the low-pass filter of the Fourier Activity, where each harmonic at f was scaled and shifted by H = 1/(1 + jf/f<sub>c</sub>). Here V<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>in</sub> = Z<sub>C</sub> / (Z<sub>R</sub> + Z<sub>C</sub>); multiply top and bottom by jωC to get 1/(1 + jωRC). Compute V<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>in</sub> at ω = 1000 rad/s, as a magnitude and an angle.

hint.text: ωRC is a plain number here. Or use your answers: divide V<sub>C</sub> by V<sub>in</sub> = 10∠0° V.

tasks.title: The cutoff frequency
tasks.prompt: Writing 1/(1 + jωRC) as 1/(1 + jω/ω<sub>c</sub>) gives the corner ω<sub>c</sub> = 1/(RC), shown in the ω<sub>c</sub> readout. The Fourier Tool works in hertz.

questions.prompt: Which Fourier cutoff f_c matches this circuit?

choices.text: f_c = ω_c/2π ≈ 212 Hz.
f_c = ω_c ≈ 1333 Hz, since rad/s and Hz are the same unit.
f_c = ω/2π ≈ 159 Hz, the source frequency.

tasks.title: Sweep ω
tasks.prompt: ω is now unlocked. Sweep it from below 400 rad/s to above 4000 rad/s, a factor of 3 or more on each side of ω<sub>c</sub>, and watch |V<sub>C</sub>| against V₀ and the angle of V<sub>C</sub>.

questions.prompt: As ω rises through ω_c, what does V_C / V_in do?

choices.text: Its magnitude falls from about 1 toward 0, and its angle goes from about 0° toward −90°.
Its magnitude rises from about 0 toward 1, and its angle goes from about −90° toward 0°.
Its magnitude stays the same; only its angle changes.
Its magnitude peaks at ω_c and falls on both sides.

parts.title: Part 3: Series RLC
parts.notes: The Setup fixes every circuit value; the first Task locks the Setup Controls (includeR, includeL, includeC, V0, R, L, C, omega) and hides every revealable circuit layer (the Circuit Mode's layers in ../layers.js); the next Tasks show Z_total, then I, then V_R, V_L, V_C and the KVL closure, each right after the Task that computes it. |I| is entered in mA. The Setup gives a right triangle: Z = 50 + j120 Ω (5-12-13) at ω/ω₀ ≈ 1.6, with ωL and 1/(ωC) > R near ω₀ so V_L and V_C exceed V₀ at resonance. The resonance Task opens ω alone; its Condition is ∠Z = 0 ± 2°.

tasks.title: The impedance Z
tasks.prompt: The loop is now V₀ = 6.5 V at ω = 1000 rad/s driving R = 50 Ω, L = 200 mH and C = 12.5 µF in series. As before, Z<sub>R</sub> = R, Z<sub>L</sub> = jωL and Z<sub>C</sub> = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC), and in series they add: Z = Z<sub>R</sub> + Z<sub>L</sub> + Z<sub>C</sub>. Z<sub>total</sub>, the current and the device voltages are hidden: compute Z in rectangular form and in polar form, then submit to see Z<sub>total</sub>.

hint.text: Z<sub>L</sub> points up the imaginary axis and Z<sub>C</sub> points down it, so their reactances subtract: Im Z = ωL − 1/(ωC). Use L in henries (1 mH = 10⁻³ H) and C in farads.

tasks.title: The current I
tasks.prompt: Z<sub>total</sub> is now drawn: check your Z against its readout. With V<sub>in</sub> = 6.5∠0° V, compute I = V<sub>in</sub> / Z. Submit to see I.

hint.text: This time Z is inductive (∠Z above 0°), so subtracting ∠Z makes the current lag the source.

tasks.title: The device voltages
tasks.prompt: I is now drawn. Compute V<sub>k</sub> = I·Z<sub>k</sub> for the resistor, the inductor and the capacitor, then submit to see them head to tail with the KVL closure V<sub>R</sub> + V<sub>L</sub> + V<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>in</sub>.

hint.text: Z<sub>L</sub> has angle +90° and Z<sub>C</sub> has angle −90°, so add 90° to ∠I for V<sub>L</sub> and subtract 90° for V<sub>C</sub>. Use I in amps.

tasks.title: Phase against the current
tasks.prompt: V<sub>R</sub>, V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> are now drawn, closing on V<sub>in</sub>. Compare each one's angle with ∠I.

questions.prompt: How do V_L and V_C sit against the current I?

choices.text: V_L leads I by 90° and V_C lags I by 90°, so they point opposite ways.
V_L lags I by 90° and V_C leads I by 90°, so they point opposite ways.
Both lead I by 90°, so they point the same way.
Both are in phase with I, like V_R.

tasks.title: Resonance
tasks.prompt: ω is now unlocked. Sweep it until ∠Z = 0, so Z is purely resistive and I is in phase with V<sub>in</sub>. That ω is the resonance ω₀, where the reactances cancel: ωL = 1/(ωC). Compare it with 1/√(LC) and the ω₀ readout, and submit with ∠Z at 0°.

tasks.title: Why can they exceed the source?
tasks.prompt: Stay at ω₀ and look at the phasor plane and the V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> readouts. Answer in a few sentences.

questions.prompt: At resonance, why do V_L and V_C cancel, and why can each be larger than V₀?
